newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia parliament defies Yeltsin on trophy art law.
newsitem.headline: Russia parliament defies Yeltsin on trophy art law.

text.p: The upper chamber of parliament urged President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday to stop resisting a draft law which proclaims Russian ownership over art seized by the Soviet Union from Nazi Germany during World War Two.

Deputies in the Federation Council voted overwhelmingly for a resolution rejecting Yeltsin's charges that there had been procedural irregularities when the bill was passed and they sent it back to him for signing.
It seemed that the matter, the latest in a series of rows between Russia's constitutionally powerful presidency and relatively weak parliament, may end up in the Constitutional Court for arbitration.

The chairman of the Federation Council's regulations committee, Valery Borodayev, said the chamber had found no irregularities in the law and that, in any case, such a decision was not for Yeltsin to take but the Constitutional Court.

"Thus the President, having assumed the functions of the Constitutional Court and refusing to sign the law has over-reached his powers and failed to fulfill his constitutional duties," Borodayev said.

Deputies also voted to send a letter to Yeltsin. The chamber's chairman, Yegor Stroyev, said the letter should mention the possibility of taking Yeltsin to the Constitutional Court if he refused to sign the law again.
Both the Federation Council and the State Duma lower chamber have overruled Yeltsin's veto on the law, which has caused indignation in Germany.

But the president refused to sign it within seven days, as stipulated by the constitution. Instead he returned the document to parliament last month because of what he called "violations in constitutional procedures" in a reference to the postal ballot the Council used to override him.
The upper chamber said on Tuesday the vote was in line with internal rules and these could could only be challenged in the Constitutional Court.

Germany, Russia's biggest trading partner and creditor, wants Russia to return art seized by Soviet troops at the end of World War Two. The vast hoard includes a rare Gutenberg bible, gold artefacts supposedly from the site of ancient Troy and paintings by Impressionists Claude Monet and Henri Matisse.

But many Russians say they should stay as compensation for the destruction of Russian cultural treasures during the Nazi invasion and for the sufferings of the Soviet Union, which lost 27 million citizens in the war.

Russia says it gave most of the captured works to communist East Germany, but only recently Moscow admitted having retained some priceless items and put some of them, including the Impressionists and Trojan gold, on display for the first time.
